summary:
Réunion is a department of France and stands under French national law without local variation: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France.

Same-sex marriage reached Réunion with the statute adopted in France in 2013, following the bill announced by Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault in October 2012 for passage through the National Assembly and the Senate, which delivered President François Hollande's campaign pledge. Both houses had to approve the text.

Discrimination on the ground of 'identité sexuelle' has been prosecutable in France since the National Assembly amended Penal Code article L225-1 in July 2012, making transphobic harassment a criminal matter; deputies Sergio Coronado and Elisabeth Pochon intervened in that debate. The provision is in force in Réunion.

Legal gender change rests on the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282, adopted by the National Assembly on 19 May 2016 after being tabled by roughly forty Socialist deputies. The government's three sub-amendments could limit the scope of that section.

Prison placement in France follows the sex recorded on the identity document under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code. Transgender women held in male prisons therefore fall into a legal grey area and are, in the account of a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018, 'punished for a lot more than their alleged crimes'; the piece follows cases including a trans woman held at Lille in 2014 amid inmate threats. That placement rule governs detainees in Réunion's prisons.

The French places-of-deprivation-of-liberty watchdog (CGLPL) found 'the persistence of serious violations' of transgender detainees' fundamental rights across French custody facilities in its opinion of 25 May 2021. The finding rests on referrals received since 2010 covering some forty transgender persons, interviews with associations and experts, and on-site and documentary inspections, and it carries recommendations addressed to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries. The opinion applies to the national framework covering Réunion.
tangentialFactors:
The 2012 marriage bill drew organised institutional opposition: the Catholic Bishops Conference came out against the adoption provision as the text moved through Parliament. Legislative support for trans-specific provisions has also been contested from within government, since the three sub-amendments tabled alongside amendment 282 could narrow the gender-change section the National Assembly adopted.

Réunion's position as a French department means that metropolitan debates over detention, discrimination and civil-status reform set the operative standard locally; there is no separate local statute to weigh against the national one.
localsOnly:
Residents of Réunion use the same civil-status procedures as residents of mainland France: a legal gender change is sought under the Civil Code section inserted by amendment 282, adopted on 19 May 2016.

Discriminatory harassment on the ground of 'identité sexuelle' is a criminal offence locally under Penal Code article L225-1 as amended in July 2012, giving residents a prosecutable basis for complaints.

Detainees held in Réunion are assigned to facilities by the sex recorded on their identity document under Article D248 of the criminal procedure code, and the CGLPL's recommendations of 25 May 2021 to the Interior, Justice and Health ministries bind the national custody framework under which local facilities operate.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports Réunion-specific enforcement data: there is no local record of prosecutions under article L225-1, of hate-crime incidents against trans people, or of the treatment of trans detainees in Réunion's own custody facilities. Whether the CGLPL's on-site inspections included facilities in Réunion is not stated and remains unresolved.

The final scope of the gender-change section after the government's three sub-amendments is not sourced here; the inventory records only that those sub-amendments could limit it.

Local availability of gender-affirming care, facility access rules and any departmental anti-discrimination guidance are not covered by the sources and are not asserted.
